narrative:
The model predicted an 80% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year grades had the strongest influence. Placing in the second decile is noticeably weaker than the average of nearly sixth-decile performance among students who were accepted, and this gap strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your family income came next; being in the upper-middle bracket actually nudged the outcome slightly toward success, because that bracket is common among admitted students. Your LSAT score of 35 was the third most important factor. While the effect was smaller, scoring below the accepted students’ average of 37 pulled the prediction modestly toward failure.

Taken together, the model saw your weaker third-year academic standing as the dominant signal, only partially offset by your family background and LSAT performance. This combination produced the high risk of bar failure that led to rejection.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your academic record. Improving your grades in later years, retaking the LSAT to raise your score, or enrolling in a strong academic-support program could meaningfully change your profile for future applications.
